papers.title: LLM-Generated Counterfactual Stress Scenarios for Portfolio Risk Simulation via Hybrid Prompt-RAG Pipeline
papers.abstract: We develop a transparent, auditable large language model (LLM) pipeline for macro-financial stress testing. Structured prompting, with optional retrieval of country fundamentals and news, emits G7 macroeconomic scenarios (GDP growth, inflation, policy rate), which are converted into deviations from an IMF World Economic Outlook baseline and translated into portfolio losses through a three-channel PCA factor model. The macro-to-factor mapping is stipulated rather than estimated, so every tail-risk multiple is conditional on stated assumptions. Across 2,420 accepted scenarios from two model families and three runs, plus an unanchored-severity run and eight risk-layer ablations, we find three things. First, severity is inherited from scenario design, not generated by the model: prompt variant dominates every variance decomposition, removing the prompted severity bands makes GPT-5.6-luna's recession 1.6 pp milder, apparent country heterogeneity largely reflects the institutional baseline, and retrieval and news matter only where the prompt leaves magnitude free. Second, numerical severity and narrative severity are only weakly coupled. Third, GPT-5.6-luna follows its own arithmetic but anchors on prompted bands, whereas Llama-3.1-8B is four to seven times more dispersed and contradicts its own stated changes in 90% of cases. A repeat run differs at the scenario level yet agrees on aggregate multiples to within 0.007 times. LLM scenario generators are best used for narrative and sector elicitation around a prescribed severity path, not as autonomous calibrators of stress magnitude.

papers.title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Pairwise Bellman Validation
papers.abstract: Model selection and hyperparameter tuning pose a central challenge in off-policy evaluation (OPE) because errors of fitted Q-functions and occupancy-ratio estimates cannot be directly evaluated from held-out transitions. Bellman-residual and minimax validation methods often require auxiliary regressions or optimization over separate critic classes, adding computational and tuning costs. We introduce pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a tuning-free minimax procedure for selecting among finite classes of fitted Q-functions and occupancy-ratio estimators using held-out transitions. PBV constructs critics from pairwise candidate differences, requiring only finitely many empirical moment calculations without auxiliary validation models or separate critic optimization. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification. Our key insight is that Q-function errors and log ratios between candidate and true occupancy ratios provide oracle critics whose Bellman and adjoint Bellman moments control estimation error. Pairwise candidate differences approximate these unknown critics, while penalties account for comparator approximation error. For Q-function selection, we first develop unweighted PBV, which evaluates pairwise Bellman moments under the offline distribution and admits oracle guarantees under a pairwise coercivity condition relating the offline distribution to the target-policy dynamics. We then develop target-aligned PBV (TA-PBV), which uses marginalized importance weighting to provide error control without pairwise coercivity. For occupancy-ratio selection, we develop adjoint PBV (A-PBV), which evaluates adjoint Bellman moments against log-ratio critics. On Hopper and Deep OPE, unweighted PBV performs competitively, while target-occupancy weighting can improve performance in settings with controlled overlap.

papers.title: Winner's Curse Drives False Promises in Data-Driven Decisions
papers.abstract: A major challenge in data-driven decision-making is accurate policy evaluation---i.e., guaranteeing that a learned decision-making policy achieves the promised benefits. A popular strategy is model-based policy evaluation, which estimates a model from data to infer counterfactual outcomes. This strategy is known to produce unwarrantedly optimistic estimates of the true benefit due to the winner's curse. We searched the recent literature on data-driven decision-making, identifying a sample of 55 papers published in Management Science in the past decade; all but two relied on this flawed methodology. Several common justifications are provided: (1) the estimated models are accurate, stable, and well-calibrated, (2) the historical data uses random treatment assignment, (3) the model family is well-specified, and (4) the evaluation methodology uses sample splitting. Unfortunately, we show that no combination of these justifications avoids the winner's curse. First, we provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that the winner's curse can cause large, spurious reported benefits even when all these justifications hold. Second, we perform a simulation study based on the recent and consequential data-driven refugee matching problem. We construct a synthetic refugee matching environment (calibrated to closely match the real setting) but designed so that no assignment policy can improve expected employment compared to random assignment. Model-based methods report large, stable gains of around 60% even when the true effect is zero; these gains are on par with improvements of 22-75% reported in the literature. Our results provide strong evidence against model-based evaluation.

papers.title: Fuji: The Shape, Composition, and Spread of Demand Bursts on Robinhood Chain
papers.abstract: Demand on blockchain-based marketplaces arrives in bursts and at a high rate. On these platforms the data are completely visible, which makes it feasible to compare the bursty demand against the usual load. The congestion manifests as an increased demand for gas, the primary resource a blockchain sells. Existing studies consider how to price the gas. The demand itself, and what it is made of during bursts, has not been measured. We measure it on Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 blockchain that quickly became a venue for trading tokenized equities and memecoins. We collected the data from every block of its first three active months and more than 50 million Uniswap swaps that occurred during bursty periods. We find that a burst trades about as many pools as a quiet period, mostly different ones, and trades them harder, on top of elevated demand that accumulated for hours. With the bursts aligned on their peaks, the median peak is 2.5 times the usual load. Both the rise and the fall of the demand are described by the sum of two exponential functions with different timescales, a slow one of hours and a fast one of minutes. Against a matched quiet period, a burst has 1.05 times the pools, 1.40 times the trades, and 1.21 times the senders. We use two models to explain the arrival of bursts: externally triggered cascades and self-excitation. The former fits the data relatively better. Inside a burst, the entry of each trader into a pool is followed for about 24 seconds by more entries than the existing traders predict. Whether this is because of imitation or because of a shared signal is left open.

papers.title: Classifying Brazilian Monetary Policy States with Interest Rate Gaps and Markov Models
papers.abstract: This paper develops a monthly framework for classifying Brazilian monetary policy that distinguishes the level of monetary restraint, changes in that stance, and statistical regimes associated with Selic adjustments. The framework combines a seven-state deterministic classifier, an empirical Markov chain, a Gaussian hidden Markov model, and Markov-switching regressions. Project outputs provide 145 classified observations from May 2014 to May 2026, with a partial final month. Under the implemented nominal neutral rate convention, restrictive states account for 88.3% of observations. A four-state HMM achieves a lower BIC, whereas the three-state model records a lower temporal validation loss. Switching regressions select three Selic adjustment regimes after solutions with degenerate variances are excluded. An additional sensitivity exercise reduces the restrictive share to 51.0% when the neutral benchmark is interpreted as real, demonstrating how strongly the results depend on benchmark measurement. The contribution is an auditable comparative application for monetary monitoring. The findings describe historical patterns conditional on the data and specifications; they do not establish predictive superiority or causal identification.

papers.title: Approximate Quantile Factor Models
papers.abstract: Weakly dependent idiosyncratic errors are standard in mean factor models, but quantile factor models have been analyzed only under independence. The mean-case definition of weak dependence, a bound on the eigenvalues of the error covariance matrix, does not carry over: I show that it neither implies nor is implied by the property that controls quantile estimation, since uncorrelated errors can share a pervasive quantile component. I instead define approximate quantile factor models through a concentration condition on the idiosyncratic array. Under it, the quantile factor analysis (QFA) estimator is consistent at a rate that deteriorates by the square root of a dependence constant, which is minimax optimal, and the number of factors is consistently estimated. Dependence changes the asymptotic variance, for which I provide HAC and thresholded estimators. Monte Carlo experiments confirm these predictions. In FRED-QD and FRED-MD, standard errors ignoring dependence understate uncertainty, most strongly in the tails.

papers.title: Multiplicity and Uniqueness of Equilibria in Continuous-Time Dynamic Discrete Games
papers.abstract: We consider multiplicity and uniqueness of equilibria in continuous-time dynamic discrete games where players move sequentially according to independent Poisson processes. With multiple equilibria, the structural model is incomplete: the reduced form and counterfactual predictions depend on how equilibria are selected. We provide closed-form sufficient conditions for uniqueness of Markov perfect equilibrium in this class of games. The conditions are semiparametric and can be verified from model primitives. To measure the coverage of the conditions and characterize multiplicity more broadly, we carry out a large-scale numerical search for equilibria of a dynamic duopoly model of entry and exit. Although uniqueness is the norm in our broad search, we find that multiplicity concentrates in economically relevant regions: where the market cannot profitably sustain both firms, where firms are very patient, and at intermediate decision frequencies that balance strategic interaction and commitment. When multiplicity is present, we typically find two stable asymmetric equilibria and one unstable symmetric equilibrium. Monte Carlo and counterfactual simulations show this structure matters for empirical work. A full-solution estimator that assumes uniqueness can converge to the unstable equilibrium, even when the data were generated by a stable one, while a two-step estimator recovers the correct equilibrium.

papers.title: Testing for Essential Heterogeneity in the Marginal Treatment Effects Model
papers.abstract: We propose a test for essential heterogeneity in the marginal treatment effects model without imposing additive separability. On the observed support of the propensity score, no essential heterogeneity implies that the conditional mean of the outcome is affine in the propensity score, and this affine restriction is the sharp testable implication of the null. We implement the test using a projected Gaussian-process statistic that is Neyman-orthogonal to the first-step estimation error, so the multiplier bootstrap avoids re-estimating nuisance parameters. Monte Carlo experiments show accurate size control and good power, and, unlike the fixed-scale integrated conditional moment benchmark, the data-driven median rule retains power as the conditioning set grows in dimension. In an application to the Ugandan ELA programme, the omnibus statistic rejects the null of no essential heterogeneity for aspirations at the midline follow-up.

papers.title: Higher-Order Marginal Likelihood Approximation for Nonlinear State Space Models
papers.abstract: Bayesian comparison of nonlinear state space models requires integrating over a growing latent state path and a low-dimensional parameter vector. We propose a marginal likelihood approximation that integrates out the states with a numerical or simulation-based evaluator and applies a second-order corrected Laplace approximation to the integral over the static parameters. The correction is expressed through smoothing cumulants of the complete-data log density and, under derivative-growth and posterior-concentration conditions, reduces the log marginal likelihood error from $O(T^{-1})$ to $O(T^{-2})$. In stochastic volatility experiments, it removes 64\% to 99\% of the Laplace error at far lower cost than simulation-based estimators. Applications to bivariate exchange-rate volatility models and to a sample of $T = 19{,}266$ five-minute stock returns find the strongest support for heavy-tailed observations and for a transitory volatility factor.

papers.title: Cordon Tolls and Urban Traffic Volumes: Evidence from NYC's 2025 Congestion Relief Zone
papers.abstract: On January 5, 2025, New York City became the first U.S. city to operate a permanent cordon-based congestion toll, charging vehicles entering Manhattan's Central Business District (the Congestion Relief Zone, or CRZ). This study estimates the short-run causal effect of the toll on hourly traffic volumes using a two-way fixed-effects difference in-differences (TWFE-DiD) strategy that compares treated CRZ street segments to untreated Manhattan segments north of 60th Street. The empirical analysis exploits hourly entry counts from the MTA's toll-meter system (4.86 million ten-minute-block records) as the primary descriptive panel and high-frequency NYC DOT Automated Traffic Recorder (ATR) data as the within-segment identification panel. The headline TWFE-DiD point estimate indicates a 40 to 45 percent reduction in log hourly volume at treated CRZ locations, with the effect direction consistent across nine pre-registered alternative specifications and concentrated in peak hours. East River bridges in the balanced panel exhibit a statistically significant 25 percent post-period increase in volume, consistent with route substitution.

papers.title: Regression Adjustment for Ratios of Treatment Effects in Randomized Experiments
papers.abstract: We study regression adjustment for ratios of treatment effects in completely randomized experiments. The existing literature adjusts the numerator and denominator separately, but this approach misses the efficiency target, loss of which matters more when richer or high-dimensional covariate information and flexible or regularized prediction methods are used to pursue further efficiency gains. We propose a two-step estimator that directly predicts the relevant transformed outcome. Using cross-fitting, our method accommodates high-dimensional first-stage prediction while keeping the final adjustment fixed-dimensional, thereby avoiding instability from a growing number of adjustment covariates. We further develop persistence-based LASSO theory that does not require sparsity, permits more covariates than observations, and allows cross-validated penalty selection under prediction-level conditions. For additional efficiency gains, our augmented two-step estimator nests the benchmark adjustment spaces and is therefore asymptotically no less efficient than the benchmark estimators, while its feasible conservative variance estimator satisfies the same efficiency ordering. Simulation studies and a real-data analysis demonstrate that our proposed estimator performs better than existing methods.

papers.title: AI in Econometric Theory: An Example
papers.abstract: This note contains a story and a paper. The paper is about the admissibility of two-stage least squares with weak instruments, a topic we have worked on together since 2019. The story is about how we (or, rather, our LLMs) wrote the paper, and some thoughts on what this may mean for our field.

papers.title: Smoothing splines with some discontinuities
authors: Giulio Cesare Gatto Ronchieri (University of Milano-Bicca
papers.abstract: We generalize cubic smoothing splines to signals with a finite number of discontinuities at unknown positions. Rather than changing the roughness penalty, we deform the domain over which it is computed: every interval between consecutive observations can be stretched by a non-negative warp, subject to a total budget, and the optimizer spends the budget only where a jump makes stretching cheaper than bending. The estimator inherits the state-space form of smoothing splines, so it can be fitted by maximum likelihood with the Kalman filter, and it also admits a fast alternating algorithm that solves a banded linear system and takes a projected-gradient step on the warps. The budget is selected by an extended Bayesian information criterion whose constant is calibrated by simulation. In a Monte Carlo comparison the new estimators reconstruct a piecewise-smooth signal more accurately than the cubic smoothing spline with discontinuities of Storath and Weinmann, at the cost of more false alarms. Two energy applications illustrate the method: the temperature response of electricity demand in Northern Italy, and retail fuel prices, whose discontinuities, changes in excise duties, are dated by public record. The three supplements follow the references.

papers.title: Informative inference on the average treatment effect with instrumental variables
papers.abstract: Policy decisions often depend on whether the average treatment effect (ATE) exceeds a specific cutoff. In instrumental variable (IV) settings, point identification of the ATE requires strong assumptions that are often difficult to justify. Therefore, many researchers shift their attention to identification of the local (L) ATE or target bounds of the ATE. Both strategies have well-known drawbacks: the substantive relevance of the LATE is frequently questioned, and the bounds are often too wide to be informative. We propose a simple sensitivity analysis that allows researchers to maintain focus on the ATE, and then discuss its connection to related bounding procedures. Based on these results, researchers can decide, in a principled manner, whether the sign of the ATE is inferable under assumptions they deem credible. The proposed strategies are easy to apply, and we illustrate their value with two real-data examples. The R package ivate implements our procedures.

papers.title: Demand Estimation with Unobserved Stockout Substitution: Exact Likelihood Maximization
papers.abstract: When a product is sold out, customers who prefer it may buy a substitute or leave without purchasing. Efficient demand estimation in this setting is challenging when inventory is observed only at replenishments, because the stockout times, and hence the products available to each customer, are unobserved. Estimating demand efficiently under stockout substitution has been a challenging problem since Anupindi et al. (1998), and it has become more pressing as the scale of such problem instances grows thanks to innovations in retailing such as unmanned stores. We provide a complete solution to this problem for the multinomial logit (MNL) model, the most widely used model of customer choice. Using a continuous-time representation of the purchase process developed in Zhou et al. (2026), we show that the exact likelihood and its gradient are one-dimensional integrals, no matter how many products, customers, or stockouts there are. Both can be evaluated at a cost linear in the numbers of products and periods. Our method estimates demand for 2,000 products from 2,000 selling periods in under ten minutes.

papers.title: Adequacy radii for stepped-wedge trials with time-varying effects
papers.abstract: Complete stepped-wedge designs guarantee eventual intervention delivery, but their final periods contain no concurrent controls. Under exposure-time heterogeneity this creates a design-analysis tension: a constant-effect analysis can be precise while targeting a design-dependent contrast, whereas an exposure-time indicator (ETI) analysis targets a prespecified time-averaged effect but may be much less precise. We develop an adequacy radius that quantifies the size of exposure-time heterogeneity compatible with a prespecified tolerance for estimand mismatch, and combine it with precision calculations to compare complete wedges with rollout-constrained hybrid designs that retain a wait-list arm. For a balanced wedge with a wait-list under the Hussey-Hughes model, the wait-list share and the correlation act on the constant-effect GLS estimand through a single scalar; we prove that the radius increases strictly with the wait-list share and decreases strictly with the within-cluster correlation, but remains bounded. Numerical optimisation and a model-based redesign of a weekend allied-health trial show that intermediate hybrids make estimand-aligned ETI analysis materially more affordable, giving a robustness-precision frontier rather than a binary choice between a complete wedge and a parallel trial. A second trial, of digital adherence support for tuberculosis treatment, has the same radius but no detectable heterogeneity; its test of a constant effect would detect heterogeneity large enough to halve the coverage of the nominal interval only 37% of the time. The contribution is a diagnostic and design principle: when exposure-time heterogeneity is plausible, retaining concurrent controls reduces the price of analysing the estimand one intends to report.

papers.title: Gini representations of skewness, kurtosis and higher-order moments
papers.abstract: We provide pairwise-difference (Gini-type) representations of higher-order central moments for both general random variables and empirical moments. Such representations do not require a measure of location. For third and fourth moments, this yields pairwise-difference representations of skewness and kurtosis coefficients. We show that all central moments possess such representations, so no reference to the mean is needed for moments of any order. This is done by considering i.i.d. replications of the random variables considered, by observing that central moments can be interpreted as covariances between a random variable and powers of the same variable, and by giving recursions which link the pairwise-difference representation of any moment to lower order ones.

papers.title: Persistence is not Independence: A structural Credibility Protocol for Distribution based Recovery in VARLiNGAM
papers.abstract: VAR-LiNGAM recovers a contemporaneous structure from reduced-form innovations under mutual independence of the underlying structural shocks. Recovery itself and bootstrap stability of the recovered edges are natural post-estimation outputs, but neither directly assesses the identifying independence assumption. We organize post-recovery validation as an ordered, non-compensatory protocol with four layers (reduced-form admissibility, distributional informativeness, independence support and edge persistence) and establish, by a constructive population result, a Monte Carlo experiment under known ground truth and a firm-level Compustat application, that the last two layers are non-nested: an edge can persist under resampling while the recovered shocks remain dependent, and independence can be supported while the leading recovered edge fails to persist. Independence support is classified operationally by a block-permutation dHSIC diagnostic on the recovered shocks, with mutual information as a continuous measure of residual dependence and tail co-exceedance as a complementary extreme-dependence diagnostic. Empirically, the conjunction of no detected independence violation and a reportable persistent leading edge occurs only in a small subset.

papers.title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
papers.abstract: Many structural breaks are announced in advance, yet adaptive conformal methods learn of them only from their own errors. A reset at the announced date serves one of two audits, conformal reliability of the next interval or frequency calibration of a closed window, and the two can disagree. For independent scores, restarting the empirical quantile at the boundary attains the minimax reliability rate, of order one over the square root of the post-break count. Restarting an adaptive recursion attains a frequency gap of order one over that count on bounded scores when its floor adds a bounded total. That gap bounds nothing about the next interval. After a large synthetic break, the restarted quantile's coverage error at the 50th forecast is 0.035, against 0.052 for the best of five adaptive baselines. The restarted recursion has the smallest frequency gap over the first 50 forecasts after every synthetic break. Real breaks are mostly smaller. The restarted quantile beats two baselines after an electricity market reform and trails all five after monetary policy decisions. Of nine announced breaks screened, only one is large enough for a detectable gain, and there every method misses nominal coverage by more than 0.1.

papers.title: Improving the accuracy of bubble date estimators under time-varying volatility
papers.abstract: In this study, we consider a four-regime bubble model under the assumption of time-varying volatility and propose the algorithm of estimating the break dates with volatility correction: First, we estimate the emerging date of the explosive bubble, its collapsing date, and the recovering date to the normal market under assumption of homoskedasticity; second, we collect the residuals and then employ the WLS-based estimation of the bubble dates. We demonstrate by Monte Carlo simulations that the accuracy of the break dates estimators improve significantly by this two-step procedure in some cases compared to those based on the OLS method and to the sign-based dating procedure of Harvey, Leybourne and Zu (2020).

papers.title: Transmission Channel Analysis in Dynamic Models
papers.abstract: We propose a framework for analysing transmission channels in a large class of dynamic models. Our method, labelled Transmission Channel Analysis (TCA), decomposes the total effects captured by impulse response functions into the effects flowing through transmission channels, thereby providing a quantitative assessment of the strength of various well-defined channels. This decomposition requires no identification assumptions beyond those needed to identify the structural shock whose effects the researcher wants to decompose. We provide algorithms to compute the effect through any transmission channel and prove that, for structural vector autoregressive models, impulse response functions are sufficient statistics for doing so. Applications to policy shocks in a variety of popular macroeconomic models demonstrate the empirical relevance of TCA for policy evaluation.

papers.title: Policy Learning with Confidence
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a rule for policy selection in the presence of estimation uncertainty, explicitly accounting for estimation risk. The rule belongs to the class of risk-aware rules on the efficient decision frontier, characterized as policies offering maximal estimated welfare for a given level of estimation risk. Among this class, the proposed rule is chosen to provide a reporting guarantee, ensuring that the welfare delivered exceeds a threshold with a pre-specified confidence level. We apply this approach to the allocation of a limited budget among social programs using estimates of their marginal value of public funds and associated standard errors.

papers.title: Control VAR: a counterfactual based approach to inference in macroeconomics
papers.abstract: A recursive VAR is read as causal whenever the policy is ordered first. I show that this ordering is not sufficient when the policy reacts to the economy it is meant to affect: the impulse response then combines the causal effect with a bias from the common trends that the policy reacts to and a bias specific to the treated unit. I develop the Control VAR (CVAR), which compares the treated unit with untreated controls that share its stochastic trends, and removes the first bias and, under exogeneity with respect to the counterfactual cycle, the second. The method allows repeated, continuous and multiple policies, separates the effect of a single policy change from that of its later values, measures the bias of a VAR without controls through the response of the controls, and bounds the remaining bias. I estimate the weights, derive bootstrap inference, show that the CVAR in changes remains valid when the treated unit has a stochastic trend of its own, test whether the more efficient CVAR in levels is supported, and characterise the bias of weights estimated in changes. I apply the CVAR to the Alaska Permanent Fund Dividend, extended unemployment benefits and California's Low Carbon Fuel Standard.

papers.title: Reevaluating Causal Estimation Methods with Data from a Product Release
papers.abstract: Machine learning methods estimate flexible relationships between confounders, treatments and outcomes, making unconfoundedness assumptions in causal analysis more palatable. How successful are these approaches in recovering ground truth baselines? We analyze new data covering an experimental rollout of a software product feature for one group of users and a voluntary opt-in to the same feature for another similar group. Recovering causal effects from nonrandomized data is feasible--but only with careful modeling choices. We offer best practices for more credible treatment effect estimation in modern, high-dimensional datasets and evaluate which tests provide meaningful signals about the reliability of estimated effects.

papers.title: Decomposition of Spillover Effects Under Misspecification: Pseudo-true Estimands and a Local-Global Extension
papers.abstract: To measure spillovers, researchers often summarize who else was treated with a simple measure, such as the share of treated neighbors. We study what the researcher estimates when that summary is misspecified. We show that the researcher estimates the best approximation to the true policy effect among all functionals of the chosen summary, and that the usual direct and spillover estimates are exactly the components of this approximation. We then specialize this framework to a setting common in applications such as cash transfers: treatment spills over both globally, through market equilibrium, and locally, through network externalities, while the researcher models only one channel. The network estimator still recovers the network spillover, and the equilibrium estimator the equilibrium spillover, even when the other channel is ignored. We illustrate with a simulation calibrated to a large cash-transfer experiment.

papers.title: Bias-robust causal inference for panel data
papers.abstract: We develop a bias-robust framework for causal inference in panel data models with interactive fixed effects. Conventional imputation-based estimators of average treatment effects on the treated do not explicitly account for counterfactual approximation error, potentially leading to misleading inference. Building on bias-aware minimax methods, we construct an estimator that corrects imputed counterfactuals using weighted untreated residuals and delivers confidence intervals with an explicit allowance for the remaining approximation bias. The resulting framework separates protection against approximation bias from the efficiency gains obtained through optimal correction. In simulations, the correction reduces confidence interval length by approximately 13\% relative to bias-aware inference without correction, while preserving empirical coverage. An application to Election Day Registration demonstrates how the correction strengthens the robustness of substantive conclusions to counterfactual error. The proposed approach provides a transparent sensitivity analysis for causal effects when the accuracy of counterfactual imputation cannot be established from observed data alone.

papers.title: Uniform Inference for Parameters Identified by Conditional Quantile Restrictions
papers.abstract: Many structural and dynamic economic models imply that key parameters are identified by conditional quantile restrictions. Building on the exponential-weighting approach of Bierens (1990) and penalized maximum statistics for conditional moment restrictions developed by Chen et al. (2025), we develop a framework for uniform inference on such parameters. We transform the conditional restriction into a continuum of unconditional moment conditions and construct an adaptive $\ell_1$-penalized supremum statistic that aggregates evidence across quantile indices. The penalty regularizes maximization over the weighting direction. Under the stated conditions, adaptive penalty selection asymptotically preserves or improves worst-case local power relative to the unpenalized test over a prespecified set of alternatives. The improvement is strict whenever a positive candidate penalty raises the population maximin criterion above its value at zero. We extend the theory to settings with pre-estimated nuisance parameters, characterizing the additional terms induced by the plug-in step in the limiting process. We derive an analytically corrected variance estimator that accounts for this estimation uncertainty and establish the validity of a Gaussian multiplier bootstrap for null inference and its shifted counterpart for analysis of local power. Monte Carlo comparisons favor CvM-KS for size control under pre-estimation and show that adaptive penalization can improve empirical power relative to the unpenalized test.

papers.title: A Balanced Parametrization of Correlation Matrices
papers.abstract: We introduce the balanced correlation parametrization (BCP), which maps positive-definite correlation matrices one-to-one onto the set of symmetric hollow (zero-diagonal) matrices with unrestricted off-diagonal entries. A key feature of the parametrization is that both the transformation and its inverse are available in closed form. It can be viewed as a generalization of the transformation underlying the classical correlation $t$-statistic to higher dimensions. It has a direct interpretation as a scaled sum of marginal and partial correlations, is inverse-consistent and equivariant under variable permutations and sign changes, and preserves block structure. A novel property of BCP is that it preserves correlation sparsity as the dimension tends to infinity under suitable factor conditions, providing a basis for sparse high-dimensional correlation modeling. An empirical illustration using standardized idiosyncratic daily stock returns for 1,765 equities over 15 years shows that BCP retains the approximate sparsity pattern and magnitudes of shock correlations, and that it yields accurate positive-definite reconstructions under sparse coordinate restrictions.

papers.title: Recurrent Neural Networks for Forecasting Autoregressive Noncausal Processes
papers.abstract: This paper examines the use of recurrent neural networks and their extensions for forecasting autoregressive causal-noncausal processes, characterized by local explosive patterns such as bubbles and spikes. We study the recurrent neural networks (RNN), long short-term memory networks (LSTM), gated recurrent unit (GRU), bidirectional LSTM, and also a simple feed-forward network (FNN) to reveal the difficulty of forecasting extreme values depending on the type of network and the length of the training set. We show that FNN outperforms other networks in predicting extreme values of a univariate noncausal time series during a bubble. We also examine the improvements of point predictions of extreme values resulting from pooling and a modified loss function.
